page.title: Best Drawing Tablet for Photo Editing (2026): Tested Picks for Photoshop and Lightroom
page.h1: Best drawing tablet for photo editing
page.desc: The best drawing tablet for photo editing is the Xencelabs Pen Tablet Medium Bundle: 10.33 × 5.8 in 16:9 area, two pens, Quick Keys dial, 16-hour wireless. Who should buy Wacom instead.
page.intro:
Short answer. The best drawing tablet for photo editing is the Xencelabs Pen Tablet Medium Bundle ({buy:xencelabs-pen-tablet-medium-bundle}): a 10.33 × 5.8 in active area in 16:9 that maps edge to edge onto a widescreen monitor, two battery-free pens with 8,192 pressure levels, and the Quick Keys remote whose dial handles brush size, zoom and Lightroom sliders. The top worry is wireless: it runs 16 hours per charge over a USB dongle that needs a free USB-A port (a USB-C adapter is in the box); there is no Bluetooth.

If you want every control on the tablet and Bluetooth with no dongle, the Wacom Intuos Pro Medium (2025) wins that segment with 10 ExpressKeys and two dials built in, but it ships one pen, dropped touch input, and lists for more. For a laptop bag or light Lightroom masking, the Xencelabs Pen Tablet Small ({buy:xencelabs-pen-tablet-small}) is the value pick: the same two pens and 8,192 levels in a 6.93 × 3.89 in area at 0.88 lb.

Size rule: a medium tablet (about 10 × 6 in) suits a 24 to 32 in monitor or two screens; a small one (about 7 × 4 in) suits a laptop. Two photographers in a Lightroom forum thread said a small tablet became a struggle once they added a second monitor.

page.after:
What owners complain about

  • The dongle eats a USB port. Three reviews (Fstoppers, Creative Bloq, AppleInsider) list the lack of Bluetooth as the Xencelabs line's main gripe. The dongle is USB-A; the included adapter makes it work on USB-C laptops but it still takes a port.
  • Only three buttons on the tablet. Three reviews call this limiting. The bundle answers it with the Quick Keys remote; the plain Medium and Small do not.
  • Quick Keys quirks. One photo reviewer found the dial stopped responding in Photoshop at times, one tester saw driver glitches with the remote, and one commenter's remote dropped its wireless link until he used the cable. Updating the driver fixed most reports.
  • Driver conflicts. Two sources found the Xencelabs driver fails alongside an installed Wacom driver. Uninstall Wacom's driver first if you are switching.
  • Wacom's 2025 Intuos Pro dropped touch. Wacom's support page confirms the PTK-470/670/870 have no touch, and forum users called it fewer features at the same price. Four Wacom forum and r/wacom posts also report Bluetooth drops, a Mac that ignores the tablet for a minute after waking, and a driver that would not talk to macOS Sequoia.
  • Is a tablet needed for Lightroom at all? Three of six photographers in a Lightroom forum thread said a mouse is fine for Lightroom and the tablet earns its keep in Photoshop brushing, dodging and burning.

Which one by need

  • Retouching on a desk monitor: the Pen Tablet Medium Bundle. Map the 16:9 area to the full screen, put brush size on the Quick Keys dial and keep a mouse in the other hand for scrolling.
  • Everything on the tablet, no dongle: Wacom Intuos Pro Medium (2025). It has 10 keys and two dials on the slab and built-in Bluetooth. You get one pen and no touch. Its launch list price was $379.95 (Wacom announcement coverage, February 2025); Wacom's store could not be read on 2026-11-06.
  • Laptop or first tablet: the Pen Tablet Small. Same pens and pressure, 0.88 lb, and it fits beside a 14 in laptop.
  • Want Bluetooth under the Wacom price: XPPen Deco Pro MW (Gen 2) pairs over Bluetooth 5.0 and includes a wireless shortcut remote; it was listed at $159.99 on xp-pen.com on 2026-11-06. Its 3:2 area leaves unused strips on a 16:9 monitor unless you crop the mapping.

Not recommended for photo editing

  • Pen Tablet Medium Bundle v2: same tablet and area; the v2 adds v2 pens and HP Anyware support, which matter for remote-desktop studios, not for Lightroom. It was listed higher than the original bundle on 2026-11-06.
  • Pen displays (Cintiq, Kamvas, Xencelabs Pen Display): you edit color on the display's panel, not your calibrated monitor, pay several times more, and add parallax. Buy one only if you draw on photos daily.
  • Entry Wacom Intuos (non-Pro): 4,096 pressure levels, a 4:3-ish 8.5 × 5.3 in area on the Medium and one pen. Fine for a mouse replacement, but the Xencelabs Small costs less and includes two pens.
